title: Mexican War of Independence
description: Armed conflict which ended Spanish rule of New Spain
wiki_lead:
The Mexican War of Independence (Spanish: Guerra de Independencia de México, 16 September 1810 – 27 September 1821) was an armed conflict and political movement that eventually resulted in Mexico's independence from the Spanish Empire. It was not a single, coherent event, but local and regional struggles that occurred within the same period, and can be considered a revolutionary civil war. It culminated with the drafting of the Declaration of Independence of the Mexican Empire in Mexico City on September 28, 1821, following the collapse of royal government and the military triumph of forces for independence.
Mexican independence from Spain was not an inevitable outcome of the relationship between the Spanish Empire and its Mexican Criollos, but events in Spain had a direct impact on the outbreak of the armed insurgency in 1810 and the course of warfare through the end of the conflict. Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Spain in 1808 touched off a crisis of legitimacy of Spanish crown rule, since Napoleon had forcefully placed his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne after the abdication of the Spanish king Charles IV. In Spain and many of its overseas possessions, the local response was to set up juntas, ruling in the name of the Bourbon monarchy. Delegates in Spain and overseas territories met in Cádiz—as the Cortes of Cádiz, and drafted the Spanish Constitution of 1812. That constitution sought to create a new governing framework in the absence of the legitimate Spanish monarch. It tried to accommodate the aspirations of American-born Spaniards (criollos) for more local control and equal standing among side with Peninsular-born Spaniards (Peninsulares). This political process had far-reaching impacts throughout the New Spain colony during the independence war and beyond. Pre-existing cultural, religious, and racial divides in Mexico played a major role in not only the development of the independence movement but also the development of the conflict as it progressed.
The conflict had several phases. The first uprising for independence was originally led by Catholic priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, who issued the Cry of Dolores on 16 September 1810. The revolt was massive and not well organized. Hidalgo was captured by Mexican royalist forces, defrocked from the priesthood, and executed in July 1811. The second phase of the Mexican patriot insurgency was led by Father José María Morelos, who was captured by Mexican royalist forces and executed as well, in December 1815. The insurgency had then devolved into a guerrilla warfare, with Vicente Guerrero emerging as its leader. Neither royalists nor patriot insurgents gained the upper hand, with military stalemate continuing until 1821, when former royalist commander Agustín de Iturbide made an alliance with Guerrero under the Plan of Iguala in 1821. They formed a unified military force rapidly bringing about the collapse of royal government and the establishment of independent Mexico. The unexpected turn of events in Mexico was prompted by events in Spain. When Spanish liberals overthrew the autocratic rule of king Ferdinand VII in 1820, Mexican conservatives in New Spain saw political independence as a way to maintain their position. The unified military force entered Mexico City in triumph in September 1821 and the Spanish viceroy Juan O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, ending Spanish colonial rule.
American Indian resistance in Mexico predates the War of Independence, including the 1761 Peasant Revolt in Puebla in response to Spanish colonial policies. Though suppressed, these movements had sustained opposition traditions. Besides, Afro-Mexicans like Vicente Guerrero and José María Morelos also played crucial roles in Mexico's independence movement in the early 19th century.
Following independence, the mainland of New Spain was officially organized into the First Mexican Empire, led by Emperor Agustín de Iturbide. This ephemeral constitutional monarchy was overthrown and a federal republic was declared in 1823 and codified in the Constitution of 1824. After some Spanish reconquest attempts, including the expedition of Isidro Barradas in 1829, Spain eventually came under the rule of queen Isabella II, who had recognized the independence of Mexico in 1836.

grok_lead: The Mexican War of Independence (1810â1821) was a decade-long armed conflict in which insurgents from various social strata in New Spain challenged Spanish colonial authority, ultimately securing Mexico's sovereignty from the Spanish Crown through a combination of popular uprisings, guerrilla warfare, and elite negotiations. It commenced on September 16, 1810, with the Grito de Dolores, a public proclamation by parish priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla in the village of Dolores that rallied creoles, mestizos, and indigenous peoples against perceived injustices of viceregal rule, sparking widespread but initially disorganized revolts. Early insurgent successes under Hidalgo and military officer Ignacio Allende were reversed by royalist forces, leading to the leaders' capture and execution in 1811, after which JosÃ© MarÃ­a Morelos y PavÃ³n assumed command, convening a constitutional congress and advocating for abolition of slavery and racial hierarchies while sustaining the fight through disciplined campaigns until his own execution in 1815. Subsequent resistance devolved into fragmented guerrilla actions led by figures such as Vicente Guerrero, amid creole elite discontent fueled by exclusion from high offices reserved for peninsulares, burdensome trade monopolies, heavy taxation, and the destabilizing effects of Napoleon's 1808 invasion of Spain, which undermined monarchical legitimacy without resolving local grievances. The conflict concluded in 1821 when former royalist general AgustÃ­n de Iturbide, responding to liberal reforms in Spain and insurgent persistence, promulgated the Plan of Iguala to unite conservatives and rebels under a monarchical constitution, prompting Spanish viceroy Juan de O'DonojÃº to sign the Treaty of CÃ³rdoba on August 24, formally acknowledging independence while establishing the Mexican Empire with safeguards for Catholic primacy and social hierarchies. Though marked by insurgent atrocities against civilians and clergy alongside royalist reprisals, the war's outcome preserved colonial-era inequalities rather than enacting Hidalgo and Morelos's more egalitarian visions, setting the stage for Mexico's volatile early republican era.
